questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093452/assets/d33f9b851125443ff738fa4c3aedcbeaf8a202d05caa06747e74262c0ae89bd9.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{2\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2{e}^{2\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{2\theta })}^{2}+{(2{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{4\theta }+4{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{e}^{2\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(4-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{-\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{-\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-{e}^{-\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{-\theta })}^{2}+{(-{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{-2\theta }+{e}^{-2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{-2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8},$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )}^{2}+{(-8\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +64{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta +60{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{4+60{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\sqrt{1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta +{csc}^{2}⁡\theta {cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-[\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
